title: Tahini halva
subtitle: a sesame-paste confection set with cooked sugar syrup
excerpt: Tahini halva is a Middle Eastern confection of sesame paste and hot sugar syrup combined and poured into a tin to set to a dense, crumbly block. The syrup must reach firm ball stage, 121 degrees C, before it goes into the tahini. Mix quickly and pour while still warm; it becomes difficult to work as it cools.
sourceNotes: Sesame halva documented throughout the Middle East and Eastern Mediterranean as one of the oldest confections in the region. The tahini-and-cooked-sugar method is the home-kitchen version of the factory process, which uses a different method of stretching the mixture.

glossaryTerms.definition: A sugar cooking stage reached at 118 to 121 degrees C. A small amount of syrup dropped into cold water forms a firm ball that holds its shape but is still slightly pliable. Used for halva, Italian meringue, and marshmallow.

recipe.freezeNotes: Wrap tightly in waxed paper and freeze for up to 3 months. Thaw at room temperature for 2 hours before serving.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps well wrapped at room temperature for up to 2 weeks. Cut into pieces just before serving.

content.text: Tahini halva is a sesame-paste confection set with cooked sugar syrup. The syrup must reach
before it goes into the tahini. Mix quickly and pour into the tin while still warm; the mixture stiffens fast and is difficult to work once it drops below about 50 degrees C.
The result has a distinctive crumbly, sandy texture. It is not smooth. The oils in the tahini separate slightly on cutting, which is normal and gives the characteristic sheen.

Line a 20 cm square tin with baking paper. Warm the tahini very gently in a bowl set over simmering water or in the microwave in 20-second bursts until it is fluid and just warm to the touch. Keep warm while the syrup cooks.
Put the sugar and water into a medium saucepan over a medium heat. Stir until the sugar dissolves, then stop stirring and clip a sugar thermometer to the side of the pan.
Cook the syrup without stirring until it reaches 121 degrees C. Remove from the heat immediately.

Pour the hot syrup into the warm tahini in a thin, steady stream, stirring constantly with a silicone spatula. Add the vanilla extract and ground cardamom if using. The mixture will thicken noticeably as you stir.
Pour immediately into the lined tin and press down firmly with the back of a spoon or a second sheet of baking paper to compact it into an even layer. Work fast.
Leave at room temperature for at least 1 hour until fully set, then cut into squares or bars with a sharp knife.

attrs.problem: Halva too crumbly and falling apart when cut
attrs.avoid: Avoid undercooked syrup; if the syrup does not reach 121 degrees C, the halva will not set firmly.
attrs.fix: Check the thermometer is accurate by testing in boiling water (should read 100 degrees C). If the halva is very soft, it may be edible as a spreadable paste rather than a sliceable block.

attrs.problem: Mixture seized and became impossible to pour
attrs.avoid: Avoid adding cold tahini to hot syrup; the temperature shock causes the mixture to seize and crystallise.
attrs.fix: Warm the tahini to at least 40 degrees C before adding the syrup. If the mixture seizes, it cannot be rescued; start again.
